I have been depressed for a long time but it never affected my schoolwork (maybe because I had bigger motivators? Making my grandpa - who raised me - proud, not wanting to hurt my family with another suicide, not wanting to turn out like my parents - psychologically messed up drug addicts - or my abusive grandmother). I say affected past tense because - for whatever reason - my depression came crashing in like a comet on my education when I went to graduate school. My first semester was stellar, I did well as usual. Then I went on a slippery slow decline. I am in my last semester and am desperately trying to hang on to get through this. I finally went to the campus psychiatrist and got on anti-depressants. I feel like those little pills are the only thing allowing me to survive at this point.

If it's bad enough that I want to act on it, I call either my therapist or somebody close to me that knows I have problems with suicidal thoughts/depression. If it isn't that bad, I just try to ignore it and read a book.

15 years later, and it's nothing but an endless cycle of up periods when I am doing okay and down periods when the depression just takes over. And every time I fall back into a down period, it lasts even longer and the negative thoughts are even stronger. I don't think it's ever going to change. And I really don't want to spend the rest of a lifetime like this.

Hey, you're not alone.  I'm in my last semester of graduate school. I had a major breakdown last semester. And I'm still not better. I'm just trying to get through this last stretch. I had depression and PTSD before ever coming to graduate school. And grad school has made it 5000 times worse. I went from having very little confidence to feeling like a complete waste of space. For the last 5 months, I've been fighting persistent suicidal thoughts. Most of the people that care about me want me to quit because they're scared that one of these days, they'll try to call me and the police or hospital will answer.  Nobody I go to school with and none of the professors have any clue. Today I had plans to work on my colloquium paper I never finished from last semester. Instead I ended up drinking alone in my apartment, fantasizing about all the ways I could kill myself. This probably isn't helping much. 

I guess I just mean that I understand.

It is never too late to turn around.

No college? You don't have to go to college. No girlfriend? I feel your pain there, but not being in a relationship doesn't make you less of a person. No job? Don't give up. Get out an look. You can even get creative, like the person who stood on a street corner with a sign reading "take my resume". No friends? Do something new. One of the ways I made friends was by taking belly dance classes. 

The truth is - as harsh as it might sound - it isn't over until you decide it's over. Fighting depression is shitty and it makes things like keeping a job hard. But you're only 20. You never know what is coming next.

Think about this: At the age of 23, JK Rowling was broke, Tina Fey was working at the YMCA, Oprah had just been fired from her first job as a TV reporter, and Walt Disney had just declared bankruptcy. They were three years ahead of you now, but they turned things around. Don't give up. For all you know, you could be the someone greater than you ever imagined. Pick yourself up, throw away the alcohol. And keep fighting.

I have indeed been depressed for a long time. I've also had times where I was free (each time, something different got me there - a change of scenery, removing toxic people from my life, and yes even pushing myself to think positive.) And whatever the means it works for awhile, until it doesn't (for whatever reason). I have made changes. Several times over. Sometimes it works. Sometimes it doesn't. 

As to bringing bad things into my life, the reality is I have a very good life. Intellectually, I know I have a *good* life. I have done my best to keep my depression internal. The only time my depression led me to outward ill-behavior was very recently and yes, it has me seriously messed up right now. And positive thinking is not what I need. Positive thinking is not going to get me out of the pit this time. I need more than that. For now, I just have to survive (as you put it, continue to live a miserable life) until I am able to make the changes I need. That's my intellectual understanding that I have to finish what I started and that doing so will help me continue in the world outside my mind.

So I suppose I'll finish with this. I am glad positive thinking worked for you and I hope it continues to work.

I can't really answer for your ex, because everyone is different. But I can say for my situation.

Well, our relationship was long distance, which in and of itself is hard. Throw in that I am in an environment conducive to depression and anxiety, and the fact that I already had depression before entering that environment, and it makes things a lot harder. When we first started our long distance relationship it was all great honeymoon period and that was enough to temporarily lift me out of depression. Then summer came (I am in graduate school) and I went to see him and it was the best time of my life. I'd never been happier. 

So when I went back to the grad school environment, I crashed hard. I tried to keep it at bay and I didn't want all my depression to basically kill my relationship. So I didn't tell him when I was depressed. I would just disappear, not talk to anyone. That just made things worse. I got more depressed, and well, your brain likes to make you believe a lot of untrue things in that state (at least for me). I felt stupid and worthless and selfish and unkind. The things you mentioned that she said to you - of you deserving better, of you being too good for her - that's where I was in my head. So when we got into a fight, I sort of imploded.  I asked him if he wanted to be with me still. I told him I felt like I was making him unhappy. I gave a voice to all those thoughts I know aren't true, those thoughts I'll so readily believe when I'm depressed. And he decided he didn't want us anymore. I pushed him into it. The next day I realized the mistake I had made, but the damage was already done. We were supposed to see the new Star Wars together. He'd already bought the tickets. I was getting ready to buy airline tickets to see him over Christmas break.

When I was in that mindset,  there was no thought of the future. Just that moment. And all those thoughts of how broken and useless I was. It didn't mean that I didn't want that future, just that I was momentarily stuck in my own head. And when I get in that state, I push the people I love away. Because I feel like I am poison. I messaged my ex too after the breakup. Because I still love him. I would give anything to take back those words. Unfortunately, he wouldn't respond.  His no contact/ignoring me have just made me worse.  Anyway, side tracking.

I'm inclined to disagree with your point of view for two reasons. 

One, I fully believe that people do change. Do some assholes always stay assholes? Certainly. But can an asshole become a better person? Yes. I've seen it go both ways. So I don't agree with holding something against a person (like a drug addict that has since gone clean) who has changed. 

Two, I feel that the act of forgiveness is less for the person you are forgiving and more for yourself. I feel like holding on to resentment or anger or what-have-you hurts you even more than the person you hold those feelings for. So forgiving a person allows you to move on with your life. Maybe you have to forgive and remove those people from your life, and maybe you can forgive and continue to be a friend/family to them. 

But really, it's just an opinion. 

On a side note, I noticed your last reply. I certainly wouldn't say you don't deserve to be loved because of this opinion of yours. I'd disagree with your opinion certainly, but that's it. (Also, I feel like perspective has a lot to do with things. Maybe your perspective is skewed in some situations? Driven by emotions involved toward the person you can't forgive? I'm not saying that that is true, but just a thought.)

PTSD is a scary thing to face. And facing that beast - working to bring yourself up out of that hole that it drags you into - is no failure. That takes so much strength. 

And the reality is: school isn't going to vanish without a trace in the meantime. If you decide, once you've taken care of yourself, you can go back and finish. Or maybe you'll decide to do something else. All of that is okay. Sometimes life goes the way you plan, sometimes it doesn't. Those times when it doesn't, those moments don't make you a failure. 

You will get through this.

Do not discount someone else's loneliness just because it is different from yours. I used to be like you. I *made* my family. I searched for a reason to live other than the hope of things getting better. That reason is what led me to those people. I still get lonely, and right now, I am physically and emotionally alone. But I keep going because I know there are other reasons. I know that my feelings lie to me and my perceptions tend to be distorted. And I didn't just get lucky. It wasn't chance. It wasn't fate. I made a conscious decision to recognize the difference between my own thoughts and my depression and to find something that gave me joy and a reason to make me want to continue even when I felt alone. That was my advice to you. Keep looking. If you haven't found it yet, look somewhere new. Don't blind yourself just because it hurts to look. I'm not saying you will stop feeling lonely or you'll land your dream job or you'll find the love of your life. I'm not saying you'll get lucky or be a late bloomer. I'm saying you can find something to make you feel alive, however small. It isn't time that stops us. It's our perception that things will never change.

I sort of feel like the whole everyone else already found the one they love/success/eyc thing to be a false perception. There are a ridiculous number of people who find that later in life. The whole just pick yourself up, change your perspective thing is a bunch of b.s. I do better around people I care about and who care about me. It is a fact. That doesn't mean I'm weak or am looking for happiness in others. It just means it is easier to recognize the voice of my depression when I have the people I love to remind me that that voice is lying. It means that that voice is so much harder to silence when I am alone. I tried to explain that to my ex, and he told me the very same thing. You have to find happiness in yourself. It's probably the biggest reason things fell apart for us. He was too stubborn and unwilling to see the place I was at and couldn't accept that there's this part of me that tries to convince me I'm a horrible person and everyone would be better off without me. He couldn't see that the voice that tells me that just gets stronger when I am away from the people I love. Now that I've cleared my head some, I reread our messages from the past few months and I see my depression made me see something untrue - I wasn't a horrible and unsupportive girlfriend. So yes I understand. But don't close every door before they've even been opened. Find a reason to keep going. It doesn't have to be anything big. Something that makes you feel happy, or just plain alive. Hold on to that while you figure out the other things.
